title: Four entered the orchard (Chagigah 14b)
hook: four sages entered the mystical garden; only Akiva came out whole
carry: enter in peace, leave in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday Honi woke after seventy years to a world that didn't know him. Your line was friendship or death.

Deep water. A subject so deep it takes over your life. A retreat that leaves one person calm and another shaken. Depth is wonderful, and it isn't always safe. The Talmud has a short, strange story, just a few lines long, about four great sages who went somewhere very deep. It calls the place pardes, an orchard. Four went in. Only one came out the way he went in.
screen: `DEPTH ISN'T ALWAYS SAFE.` → `FOUR SAGES, ONE ORCHARD.` → `ONLY ONE CAME OUT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Word scholars trace pardes to an old Persian word for a walled garden, the same word behind the Greek for paradise. Tractate Chagigah teaches: four entered the pardes. Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher, and Rabbi Akiva. Ben Azzai looked, and died. Ben Zoma looked, and was harmed; the tradition understands his mind was shaken. Acher, whose real name was Elisha ben Abuya, cut the shoots, which is read as breaking from the tradition; he's known as Acher, the other one. And Rabbi Akiva entered in peace, and left in peace. That's the whole story. It never says what the orchard was. Some readers understand it as a mystical experience, a kind of journey toward God. Others think it's a picture of dangerous study of hidden teachings. The sources are silent on the details, and the silence seems to be the point. Akiva even gave the others a warning: when you reach the stones of pure marble, don't say, water, water. Nobody fully agrees what that means, either. Centuries later, Jewish teachers turned the word into an acronym, P-R-D-S, for four ways of reading the Torah: the plain meaning, the hint, the teaching, and the secret. The orchard became the whole depth of the text. And Akiva's way through it became a model: go in, go deep, and come out whole.
screen: `PARDES: A WALLED GARDEN.` · `FOUR WENT IN.` · `ONLY AKIVA LEFT IN PEACE.` · `THE SOURCES DON'T SAY WHAT IT WAS.` · then, large: `ENTER IN PEACE, LEAVE IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: A look back at this week: my children won, these and these, Beruriah's reading, the jewels on loan, two in the desert, Honi's long sleep, and now the orchard. Enter the stillness on purpose: feel your feet, your seat, your breath, and go as deep as feels right. Near the end, come back on purpose too, noticing your hands and the room, and leave the way you came in: whole.
Pardes. An orchard, the root of paradise. Four sages entered; only Rabbi Akiva entered in peace and left in peace.
Your line: enter in peace, leave in peace. Only Akiva did both. Day two hundred eighty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition has long treated mystical study with caution, and many communities traditionally taught Kabbalah only to mature students; the PaRDeS acronym is widely used to describe levels of reading Torah.

notes: Chagigah 14b paraphrased. 'Ben Zoma was harmed' is often understood as losing his sanity; the script says his mind was shaken.
Pardes: from Old Persian (Avestan pairidaeza), via Greek paradeisos; confirm phrasing.
The PaRDeS acronym is usually traced to the 13th century (Zohar circles, Moses de Leon, Bahya ben Asher); the script says 'centuries later'.
Scholarly views on what the pardes was (mystical ascent vs. esoteric study) are summarized without ranking.
